question: A 50-year-old woman has two months of non-healing oral erosions followed by flaccid skin blisters that rupture into raw, weeping areas. Lateral finger pressure on normal-looking skin shears off the surface. Which combination correctly identifies the likely diagnosis, cleavage level, and target antigen?

answers.text: Pemphigus vulgaris — intra-epidermal (suprabasal) acantholysis, Nikolsky positive, anti-desmoglein 3/1

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. Flaccid bullae, oral erosions preceding skin involvement, and a positive Nikolsky's sign are the hallmarks of pemphigus vulgaris — an intra-epidermal disease caused by IgG against desmoglein 3 (mucosal) and desmoglein 1 (cutaneous).

answers.text: Bullous pemphigoid — sub-epidermal split, Nikolsky negative, anti-BP180/BP230

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Bullous pemphigoid produces tense (not flaccid) bullae, typically in the elderly with the mouth spared, and Nikolsky's sign is negative. This presentation — flaccid bullae, oral onset, positive Nikolsky — points to pemphigus vulgaris.

answers.text: Bullous pemphigoid — intra-epidermal split, Nikolsky positive, anti-desmoglein 3

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: This incorrectly assigns intra-epidermal features to bullous pemphigoid. In BP the split is sub-epidermal and Nikolsky is negative; these intra-epidermal features belong to pemphigus vulgaris.

answers.text: Pemphigus vulgaris — sub-epidermal split, Nikolsky negative, anti-BP180

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: This reverses every feature of pemphigus vulgaris: the split is intra-epidermal (not sub-epidermal), the target is desmoglein (not BP180), and Nikolsky's sign is positive (not negative).

overallFeedback.feedback: Remember the triad: flaccid bullae + oral erosions + positive Nikolsky's sign = pemphigus vulgaris. The intra-epidermal split from anti-desmoglein 3/1 antibodies explains all three findings.
You correctly identified that flaccid bullae with oral onset and a positive Nikolsky's sign indicate pemphigus vulgaris — an intra-epidermal disease targeting desmoglein 3/1.
